Do not stop any medicine yourself, but ask your GP or pharmacist for a structured medication review.

content:
Many people with arthritis also take medicines for sleep, bladder, mood, allergies or nerve pain. Some of these have anticholinergic effects.

This guide explains anticholinergic load and how to discuss it with your healthcare team. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

What is anticholinergic load?

Anticholinergic medicines block a chemical messenger called acetylcholine. Several such medicines together increase the total effect, sometimes called anticholinergic burden or load.

Medicines that may contribute

  • Some bladder medicines.
  • Some antidepressants, including amitriptyline, which is sometimes used for pain.
  • Some antihistamines and sleep aids.
  • Some medicines for sickness or stomach cramps.
  • This is not a full list. Your pharmacist can check your medicines.

Why it matters in frailty

  • Confusion or memory problems.
  • Dizziness and falls.
  • Constipation and urine retention.
  • Dry mouth and blurred vision.

Asking for a review

  • Ask your GP or pharmacist for a structured medication review.
  • Bring all medicines, including those bought over the counter.
  • Mention new confusion, falls or constipation.
  • Never stop a medicine suddenly without advice.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if someone is very drowsy, hard to wake or has collapsed.
  • Contact NHS 111 or your GP urgently for sudden new confusion or being unable to pass urine.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I stop amitriptyline?

Do not stop it yourself. Ask your GP whether it is still the right choice.

Do over-the-counter medicines count?

Yes. Some sleep aids and allergy medicines have anticholinergic effects.
